summary: An exchange interrupted after the money moved must resume from what it persisted
description:
Found by the TKT-158 adversarial review (findings P3-1 and P3-4), carried out of that ticket when it hit the churn cap.

TKT-158 persists a **basis** — target hold, replacement reservation, unit amount, slot, total, signed delta, price snapshot — *before* calling payments, exactly so a retry can settle the same numbers. It then does not use it on the path that needs it most: an **unsettled** replay re-resolves the price and re-submits the hold before loading the basis. A price change makes inventory reject the same hold key on a different fingerprint; a catalog outage stops recovery outright. The window this closes is the one the basis was built for — an upgrade whose charge SUCCEEDED and whose local settlement write failed.

`RecordExchangeBasis` also ignores `RowsAffected`, so a losing concurrent writer receives nil and continues with a basis it did not persist — it can then win the reservation INSERT and store a snapshot that disagrees with `order_exchanges.target_price_snapshot`.

**This is the same problem TKT-163 tracks for refunds** — *an obligation interrupted after money moved needs a durable resume path* — and the two should probably be designed together rather than solved twice.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] An unsettled exchange with a recorded basis resumes from it: no catalog call, no new hold, settling the persisted total and delta. A test drives a failure after the provider call and proves the retry completes without re-pricing.
- [ ] The resume works when catalog is **unavailable** and when the target price has **changed** — both are tested, because both are how the current path fails.
- [ ] `RecordExchangeBasis` has record-or-load semantics: the caller continues only with the authoritative persisted basis, never its own local copy. A concurrent test proves the loser uses the winner's basis.
- [ ] The resume never re-settles: a retry after a successful provider call makes no second movement. Proven against payments-side evidence, not commerce's own flags.

Quality gates: `make check` green; contract tests; money integer minor units.

binding.rule: Money is integer minor units + ISO currency code — floats are banned on money paths.

Traceability is a must, for money and tickets: money-relevant records land as immutable, hash-chained, signed journal entries from the first order (corrections = compensating entries; read models = projections), and every ticket/entitlement state change (issued, delivered, transferred, resold, exchanged, redeemed, reissued, invalidated) is an append-only lifecycle event linked to its order.

governingAdrs.why: Catalog is the SINGLE authority for the rule-resolved unit price and commerce consumes `resolved_price` without recomputing it. Any re-pricing (an exchange) resolves through catalog and persists the §5 provenance snapshot for the NEW reservation — never copies the old snapshot.

Corrections are COMPENSATING ENTRIES, never mutations. A refund/exchange appends a new signed fact; the original sale fact and its hash link are untouched. The payments journal has a DB trigger that raises on UPDATE/DELETE — any design that 'adjusts' a fact is rejected by the database, not by review.

All provider money movement goes through the PSP port. `/internal/psp/refund` and the `payment_compensations` table already exist (TKT-114/116) — the PRIMARY KEY (organizer, source_idempotency_key, kind) is what converges duplicate refunds onto ONE provider idempotency key. Reuse it; do not add a parallel refund path.

Every lifecycle event goes through store.appendLifecycle — the verifier asserts one-to-one coverage, so a direct INSERT into lifecycle_events reads as tampering and fails `access verify-lifecycle` in the gate. Canonical forms are pinned by golden literals; changing a byte is a canonical-version migration, not a test update. Also: name the adversary before writing 'tamper-evident'.

The checkout journal protocol defines how commerce records money facts (order_facts row → payments /internal/facts, deterministic fact_id, idempotent). A post-purchase money movement uses the same protocol; do not invent a second one.

Inventory's claim transaction is the contention path. Giving capacity back must go through the same row-locked transaction discipline; a plain UPDATE outside it can drive confirmed_quantity negative or double-return under concurrency.

Fail closed. Responses are validated against the spec; an undeclared status code becomes a 500. Every new endpoint must declare every status it can answer, and a downstream answer commerce cannot validate aborts rather than degrades.

Contract-first. A new operation is written in the service's openapi.yaml first, then `openapi_gen.go` / `api-types.gen.ts` are regenerated and COMMITTED before the gate runs — check-generate diffs against HEAD, so an uncommitted regen reads as drift.
Commerce and inventory ARE inside the smoke happy-path coverage gate. A new documented 2xx operation must be exercised through the running stack or the suite fails.

Migrations run out-of-band via each binary's `migrate` subcommand as a one-shot Compose job. Add the SQL under the service's internal/store/migrations/ with the next number; the server path never migrates.

objective.note: TKT-158 built the durable basis and then did not use it where it matters; an interrupted exchange can strand with the buyer charged.

scope.note: IN: resume-from-basis on unsettled replay, record-or-load basis semantics. OUT: the forward path (TKT-158), the entitlement switch (TKT-166), payments amount evidence (TKT-168).

uncertainties.note: Whether this is a handler-level resume or a runner is the same open question as TKT-163. Deciding both together is likely cheaper than deciding either alone.

dependencies.note: blocked-by TKT-158, which persists the basis this resumes from. Worth sequencing with TKT-163.

approach.note: Branch on a recorded basis immediately after the fingerprint check, before any external call; return the persisted basis from RecordExchangeBasis.

first_slice.note: An upgrade interrupted after the charge, resumed to completion with catalog stopped.

success.note: Demoable: charge, kill the settlement write, restart, replay the key, watch it finish with no second provider movement.

context_memo.note: Inherited from TKT-158. ADR-039 §1 and §3 govern; ADR-037 §5's stored-occurred_at rule applies to the facts written on resume.

comments.body:
<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
### ✅ Implementation readiness — PASS

Carved out of TKT-158 at its churn-cap stop, with the design half-built: the basis it resumes from already exists and is already constrained by the database.

**Concerns:** none blocking. One to carry: **design with TKT-163.** Both are "an obligation interrupted after money moved needs a durable resume", and solving them separately risks two mechanisms for one problem.

**Verdict:** PASS.

<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
### Gate 1 — promoted to Ready (owner, 2026-08-17)

**An exchange interrupted after the money moved must resume from what it persisted.**

Blocker satisfied: `blocked-by TKT-158` is **Done**, and TKT-158 is precisely what persists the
basis this ticket resumes from.

**Sequencing note for whoever claims it:** take this **before** TKT-168. This one fixes the
behaviour (an unsettled replay re-resolves the price instead of using the persisted basis, so a
price change makes inventory reject the retry); TKT-168 makes that behaviour *provable*. Doing them
the other way round produces a test that pins the current, wrong amounts.

**Verified before promoting, not assumed:** all eight DoR items are `met` or `deferred` with none
`open`, and every `blocked-by` link resolves to a **Done** ticket. Promoted as part of a sweep of
every fully-shaped Backlog ticket, on the owner's instruction.
